title: The Apartment Above the Laundromat
excerpt: After a flood closes her mother’s shop, June follows customer messages and city records to recover more than the lost clothes.

sections.title: The Waterline
paragraphs: When the river rose into her mother's laundromat, June Park was in a sound booth three neighborhoods away, trying to remove traffic noise from an advertisement for luxury apartments. The client wanted the city to sound peaceful. June spent two hours erasing buses and voices. By the time she checked her phone, her brother had left seven messages. The seventh contained only water and his breathing.

She reached the shop after midnight. The blue sign still glowed above a street full of brown water. Her mother, Hana, stood on the curb holding a cash box and a cardboard carton of customer tickets. Leo had carried the machines' payment drawer upstairs and was trying to keep it dry. Water lapped at the first stair of the apartment where June had grown up.

'You shouldn't have come in those shoes,' Hana said. It was the first thing she said to June after three months of strained Sunday calls. June looked at her thin sandals and laughed because the alternative was crying.

The firefighters ordered everyone back. June followed her mother to a school gym where families slept on folding cots. Hana placed the carton of tickets beneath her pillow. In the morning she asked June to check the dryers. They were still underwater. Insurance would cover some equipment, but not the wages Hana owed for the previous week or the clothes she had promised ready by Friday. June thought of the condo advertisement she had spent the day making perfect. Its building stood on higher ground beside the river, behind a wall paid for by the city.

A man in a clean coat came to the gym at noon. His name was Daniel Rusk. He owned the building and had leased the ground floor to Hana for nineteen years. He carried an envelope with an offer: take a cash settlement, leave within thirty days, and release him from repair obligations. Hana read it once and folded it small.
'You knew the drains were blocked,' she said.

Rusk said the flood was an act of nature. June had seen him at holiday dinners when she was a child. He had brought chocolates, praised Hana's work, and raised the rent every renewal. Now he looked past June to the other cots, as though witnesses made the conversation impolite.
Hana put the envelope in the ticket carton. 'I have customers' clothes,' she said. 'First I give those back.'

sections.title: Voices in the Machines
paragraphs: The laundromat smelled of silt and detergent. Volunteers cleared mud from the floor while Leo photographed the damage. June helped carry wet bundles upstairs. In the apartment she found her mother's old answering machine, a squat gray box connected to a phone line long canceled. Hana had kept it because customers still knew the number. Its small digital display blinked twenty-seven saved messages. June had once teased her for refusing a smartphone app. Now the machine held orders, pickup dates, and people asking where their clothes had gone.

June recorded the messages into her portable audio interface, cleaning each enough to hear names and numbers. A chef needed uniforms for a job interview. A retired teacher had left a quilt sewn by her sister. A father wanted a yellow dance costume for his daughter before Saturday. One caller asked for a winter coat belonging to a woman named Mrs. Alvarez. The message had been left a week before the flood. June searched the tickets and found the coat's claim tag, but the plastic bag hung empty. Leo said Hana had already given it back without charging, because Mrs. Alvarez had been in the hospital.

That small unrecorded kindness was typical of Hana and maddening for accounting. June had spent years telling her mother to write everything down. Hana had spent years telling June that people were not accounts. Both were partly right. Without clear records, the shop might have to pay for clothes it had already returned. Without listening to customers, they might return a ruined keepsake with a receipt and call the debt settled.

June made a list. She called people, explained the flood, and asked what they needed first. Some were angry. One person threatened to sue. Most asked after Hana. The chef borrowed two uniforms from a colleague and offered to help clean on Sunday. The father said the costume could wait; his daughter was scared of the river and wanted to know whether the shop cat had survived. Miso had, although he refused to come down from the upper shelf.

At dusk, June found a message from Rusk on the machine, recorded ten days earlier. He asked Hana to move stock away from the back wall because repairs to the drain would begin 'after the sale closes.' June played it three times. The lease said Rusk had to maintain the drainage system. He had known there was a problem and delayed the work while arranging to sell the building. The recording did not prove he caused the flood. It did prove he had seen the risk before anyone on the street was warned.

June took the file to a legal aid clinic. The attorney said they needed more than a phone message to challenge the release. They needed photographs, repair requests, perhaps another tenant who had been told the same thing. June returned to the shop, where Hana was scrubbing a sink that no longer drained.
'I found his call,' June said. 'You should have told me the building was being sold.'
'I didn't know it would flood.'
'You knew enough to ask about the drain.'
Hana set down the brush. 'I asked. He said he would fix it. I didn't want you to quit your work because my landlord is a liar.'
June had not offered to quit. She had offered to be told the truth. For once she said exactly that. Hana looked at the ruined floor and nodded.

sections.title: The Things a Ticket Cannot Hold
paragraphs: June had assumed the carton of tickets would tell them what to return. It told them less each day. Ink ran in the flood. Two claim tags had identical numbers because Hana had reused an old roll. A bag marked KIM belonged to one of three customers. June laid everything out by color and fabric in the upstairs apartment and built a spreadsheet. She worked through the night, delighted to turn confusion into columns.

By morning the spreadsheet had forty-eight lines and no place for the chef's borrowed uniforms or the coat Hana had given away. Hana looked at it and said it was useful. June heard the qualification. She asked what was missing.
'Who needs the clothes,' Hana said. 'Not just whose name is written on the bag.'

June went back through the messages. A young woman named Priya had left a blue blazer for cleaning before an interview. Her number was disconnected. The ticket carried only a surname and a promised pickup date. June called the hiring office listed in an old voice mail and learned Priya had obtained the job anyway, wearing a jacket from a friend. When June reached her at the new office, Priya said the blazer could wait. She had been volunteering at the flood kitchen and needed towels more than formal clothes. June crossed out her urgent flag and delivered clean towels that afternoon.

Another bag contained a child's school uniform. The name had washed off, but Leo recognized a patched knee. He cycled it across town to a temporary shelter and found its owner, a boy who had been wearing the same shorts for a week. The repair was worth little money. It was the most important item on the rack.

June added a new column to her spreadsheet: what the customer says matters. She left it blank unless she had asked. Hana watched her type. 'That's better,' she said. June pretended not to care how much the praise warmed her.

sections.title: Three Workers
paragraphs: The shop's workers did not have the luxury of waiting for the hearing. Rosa cleaned shirts before dawn, Mateo repaired machines, and Jin managed the counter when Hana took her mother to appointments. Each had a week's wages outstanding when the river came in. Hana had always paid on time. This time her cash box held less than half of what she owed.

June suggested using her savings. Hana refused at first. She thought June was offering to rescue a business that might already be lost. June said she was paying a debt to people she had known since childhood, not buying control of the shop. They wrote the amount down as a loan with no interest and a repayment date that could be extended. Hana signed. June signed. The paper made it easier for both of them to accept help without pretending money had no meaning.

Rosa asked for only part of her pay until they reopened. June insisted she take all of it. Rosa replied that she knew exactly what her household needed and did not want June deciding for her. The words stung because they sounded like Hana. June apologized and paid as Rosa requested. The remainder went into a separate envelope with Rosa's name on it.

Mateo knew the machines could not simply be dried and switched on. Motors exposed to floodwater might run for a day and then catch fire. Rusk had told Hana to clean them and resume business while the settlement was negotiated. Mateo photographed the damaged wiring and wrote an estimate. The estimate became part of the hearing file. He also found the shop's old maintenance notebook, where he had recorded standing water in the back alley after three ordinary storms. June had been looking for proof in the landlord's records; Mateo had kept it all along in a grease-marked binder behind the dryer.

Jin took charge of calling customers whose clothes might be damaged. He could hear when someone was about to shout and let them finish before explaining the plan. June asked how he stayed calm. 'I don't,' he said. 'I just wait until after the call to be angry.' They went out for noodles after a difficult evening, and June learned he had applied to nursing school. He worried leaving would make Hana's recovery harder. Hana overheard them and told him the shop had survived floods, broken machines, and Rusk. It could survive him going to school. Jin laughed, then asked whether she meant it. She did.

June had come back expecting to fix a damaged place for her mother. The three workers showed her that the shop had never belonged to one person alone, even if Hana's name was on the lease. Any plan to reopen had to include what they wanted from the work and what they could afford to give.

sections.title: The City Under the City
paragraphs: The sale documents were filed at the county office. June took a morning off work to read them. Rusk intended to sell the building to a company assembling the riverfront for new apartments. The company also owned the building beside the shop, where a florist had complained about water seeping through the basement wall. June visited the florist, a woman named Sal who kept her invoices in shoeboxes. Sal had three unanswered emails about the drains and a photograph of the back alley after an ordinary rainstorm. Water had pooled where a grate should have carried it away. The grate was sealed with concrete left by a contractor Rusk had hired the previous summer.

Sal had wanted to complain to the city but worried her lease would not be renewed. Now her flowers were ruined too. She agreed to speak if Hana would go with her. Hana said yes before June could answer for her. At the municipal office they learned that a permit for drainage work had been requested and then canceled. The reason on file was 'tenant access unavailable.' Hana had never been asked for access. The clerk printed the record and advised them to take it to the flood review board.

June brought the evidence to the attorney. He explained the practical problem: a hearing could take months, and the settlement money would pay for new machines immediately. Hana would have to decide how much risk she could carry. June wanted to tell her what to do. Instead they spread the bills on the apartment table. Leo added the wages owed to three workers, the cost of replacing customer's clothes, and the rent on a temporary space. The settlement would cover only half. Signing would surrender the claim for the rest.
Hana studied the numbers. 'I've been keeping this place open as if stubbornness were a business plan,' she said.

June said the shop had earned a chance to reopen. Hana said a chance was not a guarantee. Leo, who had heard them argue this way for years, placed Miso in the middle of the papers. The cat lay down on Rusk's offer. All three laughed, and the decision became easier to discuss. They would seek an emergency order to keep the lease while the review board examined the drain. They would ask customers which clothes were urgent and offer refunds first. If they could not reopen by autumn, Hana would decide whether the shop should end. It would be her decision, made with the whole truth on the table.

sections.title: What the Neighborhood Owed
paragraphs: The flood review board invited written comments. June drafted one that made Rusk's negligence clear, listed the sealed grate, and calculated the lost income. It was careful, persuasive, and entirely about the laundromat. Sal read it and asked why the florist was absent. The bakery had lost its freezer. The basement apartments had filled to the window ledges. June said each business could submit a statement. Sal asked whether they would all be heard separately before the city funded a wall for the wealthier block upstream.

They held a meeting in the school gym. People came with photographs on phones and damp folders of receipts. An older resident brought a hand-drawn map of every flood he remembered. His map showed water moving differently after the condo wall went up. The city engineer could not promise that the wall had caused the damage, but she agreed the drainage study had excluded the lower street. The neighborhood had not been asked to comment on the study because officials had classified the area as mostly commercial. Families living above those shops had vanished from the category.

June recognized the problem from her own work. She could remove voices from a recording until a client heard the city as empty. A planning map could do the same with a neighborhood. She helped the residents record short testimonies and transcribed them alongside the photographs. They submitted one packet with individual statements inside it, so nobody's story disappeared into a summary.

At the board hearing, Mrs. Winn spoke about carrying her quilt through two earlier floods. Sal described her ruined flowers. Jin explained how a closure affected workers who had never signed the lease. Hana was last. She said she wanted a working drain and a fair payment, but she also wanted the city to stop treating their block as the place excess water could go. Her voice trembled once. She did not apologize for it.

The board could order Rusk to pay. It could only recommend a new city study. June wanted more. Hana said a recommendation with names attached was still a door they could push. They left the hearing with a date for the next council meeting written on the back of June's hand.

sections.title: The Quilt
paragraphs: The teacher came on Sunday to help sort damaged clothes. Her name was Mrs. Winn. She was seventy-eight and wore rubber boots with flowers painted on the sides. She had not come to demand the quilt. She had come with two neighbors and a kettle. Together they made a drying line across the upstairs hall.

The quilt was heavy with river mud. Its colored squares were hand sewn, some from dresses Mrs. Winn's sister had worn as a girl. June wanted to send it to a specialist, but the cost was beyond the shop's budget. Mrs. Winn shook her head. 'Let's see what can be saved first.' For two days they rinsed each panel gently, then laid it flat under fans. The red squares bled into the white. Mrs. Winn traced the damage with a finger and said her sister would have called it another chapter of the blanket, not the end of it.

June recorded her speaking, with permission. She had begun collecting short voice notes from customers so the shop could track what mattered to them: sizes, deadlines, memories, not just ticket numbers. The files stayed on a little drive Hana could use with one button. June realized she had once imagined technology would make her mother's work efficient by replacing conversation. It worked better when it helped her remember what a conversation had promised.

Rusk came by while the quilt dried. He said the cleanup looked impressive and offered a slightly larger settlement. Hana said she had a hearing date. He glanced at the neighbors and told her privately that court would exhaust her. June played his recorded message about repairs. Rusk stiffened. He claimed it had been taken out of context. Sal emerged from the stairwell with her photographs and said she would gladly provide the context. Rusk left without another offer.

The hearing did not produce a dramatic confession. Rusk's lawyer argued that the flood would have happened even with a clear drain. The city engineer agreed the river had overtopped its bank. She also testified that the sealed grate had kept water in the shops for hours longer, increasing the damage. The board ordered Rusk to pay for the avoidable loss and to keep the leases in force while repairs were made. It was less than Hana had hoped and more than Rusk had wanted. The attorney called it a workable result.

sections.title: The First Shop
paragraphs: While the machines were being repaired, Hana found an old photograph behind the apartment radiator. It showed her at twenty-six, standing before the laundromat on opening day. The sign was white then, the windows bare, and June a baby asleep in a sling across her chest. A man stood beside her with a toolbox. June recognized her father. He had left when she was nine. She had heard the story in fragments: late payments, long shifts, one argument too many. Hana put the photograph on the table without offering an explanation.

June asked why she had kept it. Hana said the picture recorded a day when all three of them had believed the shop could hold their life together. The belief had failed in one way and proved true in another. Her father had repaired the first washers and taught Hana to fix a belt herself. When he left, Hana kept using what she had learned. She did not want June to think the beginning had been false just because the ending hurt.

They carried the photograph downstairs. June could hear the empty room echo around their footsteps. Hana pointed to the wall where she had once measured June's height in pencil. The marks had been painted over after a remodel, but she knew where they were. She pointed to a corner where Leo had done homework while waiting for the last customer. June remembered hiding beneath the folding table during a thunderstorm, safe because the dryer drums sounded louder than the rain.
'I wanted you to get out of here,' Hana said. 'Then you did, and I acted as if you had abandoned me.'
June leaned against a dry machine. She had wanted to leave and to be missed without being called back. 'I came tonight because Leo called,' she said. 'I stayed because I wanted to.'
Hana looked at the photograph. 'I know that now.'

They placed it behind the counter when the shop reopened. It was not a monument to better days. It showed a young woman beginning something she could not yet know how to finish. June found that comforting.

sections.title: The Room Upstairs
paragraphs: In August June's advertising agency offered her a promotion. It came with a larger salary and more responsibility for campaigns aimed at the new riverfront towers. Her manager said nobody knew the neighborhood's sound better than she did. June opened the sample video: the camera moved above clean windows and a bright wall, then cut before it reached her mother's street. A voice described the area as a blank canvas.

She asked whether the film could show the existing shops. The client wanted an impression of possibility, her manager said, not a history lesson. June had rent of her own and a loan to Hana on paper. She did not quit in a burst of purity. She asked to be moved to another account and showed her manager the flood review board's public findings. The client could still sell apartments; it could not use June's work to imply the street below was empty. Her manager was irritated, then practical. Someone else took the campaign. June lost the promotion and kept the job. She went home angry at the cost of a choice she still believed was right.

Hana was upstairs sorting recovered buttons into jars. June told her what had happened. Hana said the promotion money would have helped. June said she knew. They sat in the uncomfortable truth of it. After a while Hana admitted she had once turned down a cheaper lease across town because the customers who trusted her would have struggled to reach it. That choice had cost her too. She had never called it noble. She had simply decided whose time counted alongside her own.
June asked whether Hana regretted it. 'Sometimes,' Hana said. 'Especially on days when the roof leaks. But a choice can be expensive and still be mine.'

They worked late, matching buttons to damaged shirts. June played an old radio program her mother liked. The apartment was still crowded with cartons, and the shop below was not yet safe to open. For the first time since the flood, June did not feel she had to solve both floors before morning. She only had to help finish the jar in front of her.

sections.title: A New Door
paragraphs: By September, the laundromat had two new washers, three repaired ones, and a floor that sloped correctly toward an open drain. Sal reopened the florist next door. The river wall beside the condo was still taller than the one by their street; June and the neighbors kept asking the city to explain the difference at public meetings. The board ruling had paid for repairs. It had not made the neighborhood safe forever.

Hana offered June a desk in the upstairs apartment if she wanted to work there some days. June kept her sound job and brought her equipment over on Fridays. She recorded a short audio guide explaining the new pickup system in English, Korean, and Spanish, with Mrs. Winn reading one version and Leo the other. Hana insisted the recordings begin with 'Hello, neighbor.' June argued that nobody needed a greeting on a machine. Then she heard a customer smile when it played and kept it.

The first day the shop reopened, Mrs. Alvarez came for her coat. She had recovered enough to walk with a cane. Hana produced the garment from the clean rack, where it had been waiting since before the flood. June checked the tag. Mrs. Alvarez looked at them both and said her daughter had told her the coat was lost. Hana said she had put it somewhere high when the water came. It was one of the few things she had saved without thinking about its price.

That evening June listened again to the seven messages Leo had left on the night of the flood. In the first he was brisk. In the next he was scared. By the seventh he had stopped asking her to come and simply let the sound of water fill the line. She deleted none of them. They were a record of what had happened, but also of who had called for her and trusted she would answer.

Downstairs, the washers turned. Hana spoke to a customer about a missing button. Sal brought flowers for the counter. Leo complained that Miso had claimed the warmest dryer again. The building was old, its future uncertain, and the street still needed a better wall. June sat at her desk above the shop, listening to the hum through the floor. This time she left the city noise in.

sections.title: A Business Worth Keeping
paragraphs: After the hearing, Hana asked June to help decide whether the shop could last another year. Winning repairs had made reopening possible; it had not made the bills small. They put the numbers on the folding table after closing. Electricity had risen. Two machines would need replacement before winter. Rosa wanted more reliable shifts, and Hana agreed she deserved them. June expected her mother to ask for another loan. Instead Hana asked which services customers actually used and which ones consumed hours without covering their cost.

They called the customers who had offered help during the flood. Mrs. Winn suggested a repair afternoon for torn clothes, staffed by volunteers and paid workers together. Priya, now settled in her new job, offered to organize a pickup route for neighbors who worked nights. Mateo pointed out that one broken dryer cost more to run than a new one would cost to finance. Leo calculated the route's fuel and wages. June built a plan that paid Rosa and Jin for their time, included a reserve for machines, and did not assume that every act of kindness could be free.

Hana was reluctant to raise prices. She worried that the families who had come to her for nineteen years would leave. June suggested a clear price list with a small hardship fund supported by people who chose to round up. Hana said she would try it for three months and publish what it covered. They posted the new list by the door with an explanation in the same languages as the pickup guide. Some customers complained; most appreciated knowing why. The hardship fund paid for school uniforms twice in its first month. June learned that a place could be generous and still take its own survival seriously.

One Friday June stayed late to test the pickup route. She rode with Jin past apartment blocks where laundry bags waited outside doors. At the last stop, a woman who had recently broken her wrist handed them a bag and asked whether the quilt had survived. June told her Mrs. Winn was using it again. The woman said everyone in the building had worried about it. June had thought the quilt belonged to one customer. It had become a story many people carried, each in a different way.

When they returned, Hana was closing the register. The numbers did not guarantee safety. The shop might still have to change or end someday. But this time the decision would be based on what the work cost and whom it served, not on an envelope from Rusk or a hope that Hana could keep giving more than she had. June put the day's receipts in their folder and turned off the machines one by one.

The pickup route did not succeed at once. On its first Tuesday, rain slowed Jin and one customer had written the wrong building number. June called to explain the delay instead of hiding it in the schedule. The customer thanked her for calling. Hana added a space on the order form for directions people actually used, such as the green door beside the pharmacy. By the third week, the route cost less time than repeated individual trips, and Rosa could plan her shifts around it. The improvement came from making small errors visible before they became someone else's problem.

sections.title: The Next Rain
paragraphs: The first heavy rain after reopening arrived in October. June was at work when Leo sent a photograph of the river. She left early and reached the shop while customers were still folding clothes. Hana had raised the baskets from the floor. Mateo checked the new drain with a flashlight. Sal stood outside the florist in boots, watching water rush toward the grate. It swallowed the stream and carried it away as designed.

No one cheered. The last flood had taught them not to trust one clear drain as a promise. June checked the city's rain gauge and called the number on the new flood notice. This time a person answered and could tell her when the mobile barrier crew would arrive. The crew was late by twenty minutes. Sal recorded the delay. Jin, home from his nursing classes for the weekend, brought tea and checked on Mrs. Winn, who disliked storms since losing her sister's quilt for two days.

At midnight the river stopped rising. Customers who had stayed in the shop helped lower the baskets. Hana reopened the dryers and offered anyone stranded a chair. June thought of the condo advertisement again, the one that had wanted her to erase traffic and voices. The room around her was full of inconvenient sound: wet boots, a machine starting badly, people calling home. It was also full of people who knew what to do when water returned.

The next morning the city crew came back to inspect the barrier. June and Sal showed them the recorded delay. The crew leader apologized and changed the deployment plan. It was a small correction, not a victory speech. June wrote it into the neighborhood's shared flood log. The log had started as evidence for the hearing. Now it helped them prepare for the next storm without waiting to be surprised.
Hana found June at the counter as dawn lit the street. 'You can go home,' she said.

'I am home,' June answered, then looked at her own damp clothes and laughed. She had an apartment across town and a life beyond the shop. The sentence was true anyway. Hana poured two cups of coffee. They watched the river recede, leaving its marks where everyone could see them.
